title: Raw search log
context: An analyst starts an investigation by scanning raw search activity in the order it happened.
task: Pull the query text, the date it was searched and whether it led to a click, for every search, with the oldest activity first.
hint: No rows are filtered out here, but the log has to read in time order — pick the field that sequences events and add a unique tiebreaker so the ordering never wobbles.
answer: SELECT query, search_date, clicked FROM searches ORDER BY search_date, search_id;

title: Searches that found nothing
context: When a search comes back empty it is a warning sign for search quality.
task: Give the search_id and query for every search that returned no results whatsoever.
hint: "Found nothing" is a specific value in the results-count column — keep only those rows.
answer: SELECT search_id, query FROM searches WHERE results_count = 0;

title: Mobile audience in India
context: A product team is planning a mobile-first push in the Indian market.
task: List the user_id and email of users who are on a mobile device and based in India.
hint: Both traits have to be true of the same user at once.
answer: SELECT user_id, email FROM users WHERE device = 'mobile' AND country = 'India';

title: Currently-serving campaigns
context: The ads desk only wants to see the campaigns that are live right now.
task: Return the advertiser and budget for every campaign that is currently running.
hint: A campaign's state is a text label — match the one that means it is live.
answer: SELECT advertiser, budget FROM ad_campaigns WHERE status = 'active';

title: Commercial-intent verticals
context: Shopping and Travel are the two highest commercial-intent categories.
task: Return the advertiser and category for campaigns that sit in either the Shopping or the Travel category.
hint: The category has to be one of a short set of allowed values.
answer: SELECT advertiser, category FROM ad_campaigns WHERE category IN ('Shopping','Travel');

title: Instructional searches
context: Queries phrased as instructions signal how-to intent for the content team.
task: Return the query for every search that opens with the words 'how to'.
hint: Pattern-match the start of the query text.
answer: SELECT query FROM searches WHERE query LIKE 'how to%';

title: Local-intent searches
context: Queries that hint at a nearby place feed the local-results ranking.
task: Return the search_id and query for searches that mention 'near me' or 'nearest' anywhere in the text.
hint: The phrase can sit anywhere inside the query, and there are two wordings to catch.
answer: SELECT search_id, query FROM searches WHERE query LIKE '%near me%' OR query LIKE '%nearest%';

title: Top of the org chart
context: The person at the very top of the company reports to no one.
task: Return the name and level of any employee who has no manager above them.
hint: A missing manager is the absence of a value, not a zero or a blank.
answer: SELECT name, level FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL;

title: March 2025 activity
context: The team is closing out the month of March 2025.
task: Return the search_id and search_date for every search that took place during March 2025.
hint: Dates are stored as ISO text, so an inclusive range works — figure out the first and last day of the month.
answer: SELECT search_id, search_date FROM searches WHERE search_date BETWEEN '2025-03-01' AND '2025-03-31';

title: Advertisers by spend power
context: Sales ranks advertisers by how much money they have committed.
task: Return advertiser and budget with the biggest budgets at the top, breaking ties by advertiser name.
hint: Sort on the budget from high to low, then add a name tiebreaker so equal budgets stay in a stable order.
answer: SELECT advertiser, budget FROM ad_campaigns ORDER BY budget DESC, advertiser;

title: Five highest earners
context: A compensation review starts with the people at the top of the pay scale.
task: Return the name, level and salary of the five best-paid employees, breaking ties by name.
hint: Sort by pay from high to low, then keep only the top handful.
answer: SELECT name, level, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC, name LIMIT 5;

title: Daily burn rate
context: Pacing a campaign means knowing how much budget it can spend each day.
task: Return the advertiser and daily_budget (to 2 decimals): the total budget divided by the number of days the campaign runs.
hint: You need the gap in days between the start and end dates — there is a way to turn two dates into a day count you can divide by.
answer: SELECT advertiser, ROUND(budget / (julianday(end_date) - julianday(start_date)), 2) AS daily_budget FROM ad_campaigns;

title: How specific is the query?
context: Longer, multi-word queries usually mean a more specific need.
task: Return the query and word_count: how many words it contains (the number of spaces, plus one).
hint: There is no word function — infer the count from how many spaces the text holds by comparing its length with and without them.
answer: SELECT query, LENGTH(query) - LENGTH(REPLACE(query, ' ', '')) + 1 AS word_count FROM searches;

title: Hour of day
context: Traffic patterns depend on which hour searches happen in.
task: Return the search_id and the hour, as a whole number, taken from each search_time (stored as 'HH:MM').
hint: Grab the first two characters of the time text and turn that piece into a number.
answer: SELECT search_id, CAST(SUBSTR(search_time, 1, 2) AS INTEGER) AS hour FROM searches;

title: Advertiser labels in caps
context: A report renders advertiser names in all capitals.
task: Return each campaign's advertiser name in upper case, aliased as advertiser_upper.
hint: There is a function that forces text to capitals.
answer: SELECT UPPER(advertiser) AS advertiser_upper FROM ad_campaigns;

title: Intent mix
context: Product wants to see how search demand splits across categories.
task: Return each category and the number of searches that fall in it.
hint: Collapse the rows to one per category, then count how many landed in each.
answer: SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS searches FROM searches GROUP BY category;

title: Ad slot usage
context: The ads team checks how impressions spread across the slot positions.
task: Return each ad position and how many impressions ran in it, listed from the top slot downward.
hint: One row per position; count within each, then sort by the slot number.
answer: SELECT position, COUNT(*) AS impressions FROM ad_impressions GROUP BY position ORDER BY position;

title: How varied is demand?
context: The number of unique queries shows how diverse search demand really is.
task: Return distinct_queries: how many different query strings appear across all searches.
hint: The same query is searched many times — each distinct one should be counted only once.
answer: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT query) AS distinct_queries FROM searches;

title: Total ad spend
context: Finance needs the total money collected from ad clicks.
task: Return ad_revenue: the combined cost of every impression, to 2 decimals.
hint: Add up the cost column across all impressions.
answer: SELECT ROUND(SUM(cost), 2) AS ad_revenue FROM ad_impressions;

title: Overall click-through rate
context: CTR is the share of searches that ended in a click.
task: Return ctr_pct: the percentage of searches that were clicked, to 1 decimal.
hint: The clicked flag is 0 or 1, so its average is already a rate — scale that up to a percentage.
answer: SELECT ROUND(AVG(clicked) * 100, 1) AS ctr_pct FROM searches;

title: Pay by level
context: HR benchmarks the typical pay in each level band.
task: Return each level and its average salary as a whole number, ordered by level.
hint: Average the pay within each level, then round away the decimals.
answer: SELECT level, ROUND(AVG(salary)) AS avg_salary FROM employees GROUP BY level ORDER BY level;

title: Campaign calendar span
context: Ops wants the outer bounds of the whole campaign calendar.
task: Return first_start (the earliest start date) and last_end (the latest end date) across all campaigns, in a single row.
hint: The smallest and the largest date value, side by side.
answer: SELECT MIN(start_date) AS first_start, MAX(end_date) AS last_end FROM ad_campaigns;

title: Device split
context: The device breakdown drives design priorities.
task: Return each device type and how many users are on it.
hint: One row per device; count the users in each.
answer: SELECT device, COUNT(*) AS users FROM users GROUP BY device;

title: Org sizes
context: Leadership tracks headcount across the orgs.
task: Return each org and its headcount.
hint: One row per org; count the employees in each.
answer: SELECT org, COUNT(*) AS headcount FROM employees GROUP BY org;

title: Spend per campaign
context: Each campaign's consumed budget matters for pacing.
task: Return campaign_id and spend: the total cost that campaign has accrued, to 2 decimals.
hint: Add up cost within each campaign.
answer: SELECT campaign_id, ROUND(SUM(cost), 2) AS spend FROM ad_impressions GROUP BY campaign_id;

title: Does slot position help?
context: The team suspects higher ad slots earn more clicks.
task: Return each position and its ctr_pct (percentage of impressions clicked, to 1 decimal), ordered by position.
hint: Average the 0/1 click flag within each position and scale it to a percentage.
answer: SELECT position, ROUND(AVG(clicked) * 100, 1) AS ctr_pct FROM ad_impressions GROUP BY position ORDER BY position;

title: Most-searched queries
context: The trends board features the queries people search most.
task: Return the query and its search count for the five most-searched queries, breaking ties by query.
hint: Count per query, put the busiest at the top, then keep only the top few.
answer: SELECT query, COUNT(*) AS searches FROM searches GROUP BY query ORDER BY searches DESC, query LIMIT 5;

title: Power searchers
context: Heavy users are a segment worth studying on their own.
task: Return the user_id and search count for users who made more than 12 searches.
hint: The condition is on each user's total, so it applies after the rows are grouped — not to individual searches.
answer: SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS searches FROM searches GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 12;

title: Readable impression log
context: Raw impressions carry only a campaign id, not the advertiser name.
task: Return the impression_id, the advertiser and the cost for every impression.
hint: The advertiser lives on the campaigns table — link each impression to its campaign to pull it in.
answer: SELECT i.impression_id, c.advertiser, i.cost FROM ad_impressions i JOIN ad_campaigns c ON c.campaign_id = i.campaign_id;

title: Desktop search behaviour
context: A study focuses on how desktop users search.
task: Return the search_id and query for searches made by users on a desktop device.
hint: The device is a property of the user, not the search — connect the two tables, then filter.
answer: SELECT s.search_id, s.query FROM searches s JOIN users u ON u.user_id = s.user_id WHERE u.device = 'desktop';

title: Clicks by advertiser
context: The team wants to know which advertisers attract the most clicks.
task: Return each advertiser and their total number of clicks.
hint: Link impressions to their campaign, then total the click flag for each advertiser.
answer: SELECT c.advertiser, SUM(i.clicked) AS clicks FROM ad_impressions i JOIN ad_campaigns c ON c.campaign_id = i.campaign_id GROUP BY c.advertiser;

title: Demand by country
context: A map widget ranks search demand by country.
task: Return each country and its search count, busiest country first, breaking ties by country name.
hint: Country is on the users table — join searches to users, group by country, and rank by the count.
answer: SELECT u.country, COUNT(*) AS searches FROM searches s JOIN users u ON u.user_id = s.user_id GROUP BY u.country ORDER BY searches DESC, u.country;

title: Result-page depth
context: Result pages are labelled by how full they came back.
task: Return the search_id and a bucket label: 'none' when there were no results, 'few' when under 100, and 'many' otherwise.
hint: Test the result count in tiers, working from the zero case upward.
answer: SELECT search_id, CASE WHEN results_count = 0 THEN 'none' WHEN results_count < 100 THEN 'few' ELSE 'many' END AS bucket FROM searches;

title: Monthly search volume
context: The trend chart plots search volume month by month.
task: Return the month as YYYY-MM and the number of searches in each, ordered chronologically.
hint: Format each date down to just its year and month, then group on that value.
answer: SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', search_date) AS month, COUNT(*) AS searches FROM searches GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;
